rows.name: context-16-frozen-16
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Because a timeout means the client does not know whether the charge happened, not that it failed. A retry with the same durable idempotency key identifies the same operation; the server must prevent concurrent execution and return the saved result if it already completed. The charge and its durable outcome record must commit atomically when they share a transactional system, so a crash cannot leave a completed charge with no record. If an external provider performs the charge, a local database transaction alone cannot guarantee that: the provider must also deduplicate using a stable key, and the server must recover or reconcile the outcome rather than submit a fresh charge.

review.note: Timeout conveys unknown outcome, stable durable key/atomic exclusion and recorded outcome close local gap; external charge requires provider dedup/reconciliation, no invented local atomicity guarantee.
review.usefulPrefix: Because a timeout means the client does not know whether the charge happened, not that it failed. A retry with the same durable idempotency key identifies the same operation; the server must prevent concurrent execution and return the saved result if it already completed.

rows.name: context-21-frozen-21
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Because compare-and-swap applies your update only if the current value matches your expectation; an obsolete expectation can keep failing, and a stale desired value can overwrite intervening progress. For an increment, if you expected 5 but failure reveals 7, retry expecting 7 and proposing 8—not 6. In C++, failed compare_exchange updates the expected argument with the observed value, so recompute the desired value before retrying; compare_exchange_weak can also fail spuriously, even when the values match.

review.note: Actual frozen CAS expected5 failureobserved7 requires expected7/proposal8, notstale6; weak spurious failure correctly qualified.

rows.name: context-27-frozen-27
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: A circular buffer gives the bounded FIFO constant-time push and pop while enforcing the capacity of 17 without overwriting queued items. Push rejects an item when all 17 slots are occupied; pop fails when the queue is empty, and advancing indices modulo 17 preserves FIFO order while reusing freed slots. The tests check those boundaries, verify that overflow rejection leaves existing items intact, and exercise wraparound to catch indexing errors that a simple fill-and-drain test might miss.

rows.name: context-30-frozen-30
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing; it does not prevent concurrent transactions from making decisions using overlapping, stale snapshots. Start with Alice and Bob both on call: transaction A reads both rows, checks that Bob is on call, and takes Alice off call; transaction B reads the same initial snapshot, checks that Alice is on call, and takes Bob off call. Under snapshot isolation, they write different rows, so both can commit, leaving nobody on call—even though each entire read-check-write operation was atomic. This is not serializable: in either serial execution order, the second transaction would see the first person already off call and fail its check. Serializable isolation, or coordination that forces these transactions to conflict, is needed to prevent that write skew.

review.note: All-or-nothing distinguished from serial order; concrete old Alice/Bob-on snapshots, disjoint own-off writes, bothcommitzero and serialsecondguard failure.
